Title: Rome in World Time, Part 5: Strongmen: From Spartacus to Actium (78–27 BC)

Summary: The last fifty years of the Republic: a rebel Roman state in Spain, Spartacus' slave army, Pompey's conquest of the East, Catiline's conspiracy, Caesar's eight years in Gaul, Crassus' death at Carrhae, civil war, the Ides of March, and Octavian's victory at Actium. Elsewhere, Han China took control of Central Asian oasis states, a Dacian king was assassinated in the same year as Caesar, and the Maya world carved the earliest known Long Count date.

---

This is the most famous half-century in Roman history, and it is famous partly because we have so much evidence. Cicero's speeches and nearly 900 of his letters survive, along with Caesar's own war memoirs and Sallust's histories. For once we can watch Roman politics almost week by week.

## After Sulla: rebellions everywhere (78–71 BC)

| Year (BC) | Event |
|---|---|
| 78–77 | Consul **Lepidus** (father of the later triumvir) tries to undo Sulla's system and marches on Rome. Defeated |
| 80–72 | **Sertorius**, a Marian general, rules much of Spain with Lusitanian and Celtiberian support, with his own senate. Pompey and Metellus fight him for years. In 73 he is assassinated by his officer Perperna at a banquet; Pompey beats Perperna in 72 |
| 75 or 74 | Young **Julius Caesar** is captured by pirates. He promises to crucify them; after the ransom is paid he does exactly that |
| 74 | King Nicomedes IV leaves **Bithynia** to Rome; Mithridates invades. Third Mithridatic War begins (to 63) |
| **73–71** | **Spartacus**, a Thracian gladiator, escapes from a school at Capua with about 70 others. His army grows to tens of thousands, beats several Roman armies and roams Italy for two years |
| 71 | **Crassus** crushes Spartacus in Lucania. 6,000 captives are crucified along the Via Appia from Capua to Rome. Pompey kills fleeing survivors and claims credit |
| 70 | Pompey and Crassus are consuls; the tribunes' powers are restored. Cicero prosecutes the corrupt governor **Verres** of Sicily |

## Pompey the Great (67–62 BC)

- **67 BC:** the Lex Gabinia gives Pompey a huge command against Mediterranean **pirates**, who had even raided Ostia. He clears the sea in about three months.
- **68–67 BC:** in Armenia, the general Lucullus' army **mutinies**, stirred up by his own brother-in-law, the young aristocrat **Publius Clodius**. Lucullus loses his command.
- **66–63 BC:** Pompey takes over the East. Mithridates flees and dies in 63. Pompey makes **Syria** a province (64), ends the Seleucid dynasty, and in 63 storms **Jerusalem** and walks into the Holy of Holies of the Temple.

## Cicero and Catiline (63–62 BC)

In 63 BC **Cicero** was consul. The bankrupt aristocrat **Catiline**, who had lost the elections, planned a coup with debt cancellation as its slogan. Cicero exposed him in four speeches ("How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?"). Five conspirators were executed in Rome without trial, a decision that later got Cicero exiled. Catiline died fighting at **Pistoria** in early 62. The future emperor Augustus was born in September 63.

## The First Triumvirate and the conquest of Gaul (60–50 BC)

Around 60 BC **Pompey, Crassus and Caesar** made a private alliance to get what each wanted. Caesar became consul in 59 and then governor of Gaul.

| Year (BC) | Gallic War |
|---|---|
| 58 | Caesar stops the migrating Helvetii and drives the Germanic king Ariovistus back across the Rhine |
| 57 | Conquest of the Belgae in the north |
| 56 | Naval war against the Veneti of Brittany |
| 55 | Caesar bridges the **Rhine** in ten days and makes his first landing in **Britain** |
| 54 | Second British expedition. Ambiorix of the Eburones destroys fifteen Roman cohorts in the winter |
| 53 | Caesar's revenge on the Eburones |
| 52 | **Vercingetorix** unites Gaul in revolt; beats Caesar at Gergovia; surrenders after the siege of **Alesia** |
| 51–50 | Final resistance at Uxellodunum (Caesar cuts off the hands of the defenders) |

Plutarch says a million Gauls died and another million were enslaved. Those figures cannot be checked, but the conquest was clearly devastating.

### Back in Rome: gang warfare

The 50s BC in Rome were dominated by street gangs led by **Clodius** (for the populists) and **Milo** (for the conservatives). Cicero was exiled in 58 and recalled in 57. In January 52 Milo's men killed Clodius on the Via Appia. Clodius' supporters burned the Senate house as his funeral pyre, and Pompey was made sole consul to restore order.

### Carrhae (53 BC)

Crassus wanted military glory to match his partners. He invaded **Parthia** and in June 53 BC was destroyed at **Carrhae** by the Parthian general **Surena**, whose horse archers were resupplied with arrows by camel train. About 20,000 Romans died and 10,000 were captured; Crassus was killed during a parley. The Parthian court reportedly received his head during a performance of Euripides' *Bacchae*.

With Crassus dead and Pompey's wife Julia (Caesar's daughter) dead in 54, the alliance fell apart.

## Civil war and the Ides of March (49–44 BC)

| Date (BC) | Event |
|---|---|
| Jan 49 | Caesar crosses the **Rubicon** with one legion: "the die is cast." Pompey and much of the Senate flee to Greece |
| 49 | Caesar beats Pompey's generals in Spain. The **Ninth Legion mutinies** at Placentia; Caesar threatens decimation and executes 12 ringleaders |
| Aug 48 | **Pharsalus**: Caesar beats Pompey |
| Sept 48 | Pompey is murdered on landing in **Egypt** |
| 48–47 | Caesar is besieged in Alexandria and sides with **Cleopatra VII** against her brother. Part of the city, possibly including some of the Library's holdings, burns |
| 47 | Zela: Caesar beats Pharnaces of Pontus in five days ("I came, I saw, I conquered"). Back in Italy the **Tenth Legion mutinies**; Caesar addresses them as "citizens" instead of "soldiers" and shames them into obedience |
| 46 | Thapsus in Africa; **Cato** kills himself at Utica rather than accept Caesar's pardon. Caesar holds four triumphs and reforms the calendar |
| 45 | Munda in Spain, the last battle against the Pompeians. The **Julian calendar** starts on 1 January 45 |
| Feb 44 | Caesar becomes **dictator for life** |
| **15 Mar 44** | About 60 senators led by **Brutus** and **Cassius** stab Caesar to death in the Theatre of Pompey |

## The Second Triumvirate and Actium (44–27 BC)

| Date (BC) | Event |
|---|---|
| 44 | Caesar's 18-year-old great-nephew **Octavian** is named his heir |
| 43 | Mutina: the Senate's armies beat **Mark Antony**, but both consuls die. Octavian marches on Rome and takes the consulship. **Second Triumvirate** of Antony, Octavian and Lepidus is made law; new proscriptions; **Cicero** is killed (7 December) |
| 42 | **Philippi**: Brutus and Cassius are defeated and kill themselves. Caesar is officially deified |
| 41–40 | **Perusine War**: Antony's brother and wife Fulvia raise Italy against Octavian; Perusia is starved and burned |
| 40 | The Parthians and a renegade Roman, Labienus, overrun Syria and Judea. Rome names **Herod** king of Judea |
| 38–36 | War with **Sextus Pompeius**, Pompey's son, who controls Sicily and starves Rome with his fleet. 36: Naulochus; Lepidus tries to take Sicily for himself, his troops desert him, and he is retired |
| 36 | Antony's invasion of Parthia goes badly; he loses perhaps a third of his army |
| 34 | The **Donations of Alexandria**: Antony gives Roman provinces to Cleopatra and her children |
| 32 | Octavian publishes Antony's will; Rome declares war on Cleopatra |
| **2 Sept 31** | **Actium**: Agrippa beats Antony and Cleopatra at sea |
| 30 | Alexandria falls; Antony and Cleopatra kill themselves. Caesarion is executed. **Egypt** becomes Octavian's personal province |
| 29 | Triple triumph; the doors of the Temple of Janus are closed, signifying peace |
| **16 Jan 27** | The Senate gives Octavian the name **Augustus**. Historians date the Empire from here |

## Meanwhile, around the world

| Date (BC) | Where | What happened | Rome at that moment |
|---|---|---|---|
| c. 82–44 | Dacia (Romania) | **Burebista** unites the Dacians into a powerful kingdom | Sulla to Caesar |
| c. 85–60 | India | Maues, first major Indo-Scythian king in Gandhara | Sertorius, Spartacus |
| 67–63 | Judea | Hasmonean brothers Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II fight a civil war | Pompey intervenes, takes Jerusalem (63) |
| **60** | China/Central Asia | Han establishes the **Protectorate of the Western Regions** to control the Tarim Basin oasis states | **First Triumvirate** |
| 57 (trad.) | Korea | Traditional founding of **Silla** | Caesar conquering the Belgae |
| 57 (trad.) | India | Start of the **Vikram Samvat** era, still used in Nepal and India | |
| 53 | Mesopotamia | Parthian victory at **Carrhae** (Orodes II, Surena) | |
| 51 | Steppe | Xiongnu leader Huhanye submits to Han; the Xiongnu split | Alesia just won |
| 51 | Egypt | Cleopatra VII becomes queen | |
| **44** | Dacia | **Burebista is assassinated** by his own nobles | **Caesar is assassinated** |
| 37 (trad.) | Korea | Traditional founding of **Goguryeo** | Triumvirate |
| **36** | Central Asia | **Battle of Zhizhi**: a Han army kills the Xiongnu leader Zhizhi near Talas | Antony's Parthian disaster |
| **36** (Dec) | Mexico | Stela 2 at **Chiapa de Corzo** carries the earliest known **Long Count** date in Mesoamerica | |
| 37 | Judea | Herod takes Jerusalem | War with Sextus Pompeius |
| c. 30s | Arabia | The Nabataean kingdom thrives at **Petra** | |
| c. 1st c. BC | Ethiopia/Sudan | Kush at Meroë flourishes; Queen Amanirenas will soon fight Rome (Part 6) | |

## Things you might not have known happened at the same time

**Two assassinated rulers in 44 BC.** Burebista, who had built a Dacian kingdom large enough that Caesar was planning a campaign against it, was murdered by his own nobles in the same year as Caesar. Both kingdoms fell into rival factions afterwards.

**Did Roman soldiers fight Han soldiers in 36 BC?** The historian Homer Dubs proposed in the 1950s that some of Crassus' captured soldiers ended up fighting for the Xiongnu at Zhizhi, where Chinese sources describe a "fish-scale" formation and a double palisade, and that survivors were settled at a Chinese town called Liqian. It is a great story, but most scholars think the evidence does not support it, and DNA studies of Liqian villagers have found no Roman link.

**Han China took Central Asia the same year Caesar, Pompey and Crassus took Rome.** In 60 BC Han set up a protectorate over the oasis states of the Tarim Basin. Silk was now flowing west in quantity; by the 40s BC Romans were wearing it, and moralists were complaining.

**The Maya calendar was getting started.** While Octavian and Antony were dividing the Roman world, someone in Chiapas carved a date in what we call the Long Count, the calendar system the Classic Maya would make famous.

**Caesar's calendar is still the base of ours.** The Julian calendar started in 45 BC. The Gregorian reform of 1582 was a correction, not a replacement.

## What comes next

Part 6: Augustus builds the Principate, loses three legions in the Teutoburg Forest, and his successors Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius and Nero follow. In China, a usurper founds a new dynasty in the very year of Teutoburg, and Vietnam's Trưng sisters revolt the same year Claudius invades Britain.

## Sources and notes

- Cicero, *Letters to Atticus*, *Letters to Friends*, speeches *Against Catiline*, *Against Verres*, *Philippics*.
- Caesar, *The Gallic War* and *The Civil War*.
- Sallust, *The Conspiracy of Catiline*.
- Plutarch, *Lives* of Crassus (Carrhae, Spartacus), Pompey, Caesar, Cicero, Antony, Sertorius.
- Appian, *Civil Wars*, Books 1–5; Cassius Dio, Books 36–53.
- Ban Gu, *Han Shu* (Book of Han), for the Western Regions and Zhizhi.
- Homer H. Dubs, *A Roman City in Ancient China* (1957), for the Liqian theory; see also skeptical reviews in later scholarship.
- Overview: [Spartacus (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spartacus), [Battle of Carrhae (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Carrhae), [Battle of Actium (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Actium), [Mesoamerican Long Count calendar (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerican_Long_Count_calendar).

**Flags:** The traditional founding dates of Silla (57 BC), Goguryeo (37 BC) and Baekje (18 BC) come from the 12th-century *Samguk Sagi* and are not reliable. The extent of damage to the Library of Alexandria in 48 BC is disputed; it was not destroyed at one stroke. Plutarch's figures for Gallic casualties are not verifiable. The Liqian "lost legion" story is very likely a myth.
